GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Move the four dots to change a circle and the lines around it, and see whether the red line always cuts the green chord in half.
How to play: Drag O, Bo, T or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claim to test what you see.
Look for the math

This is Proposition 10 of Archimedes' Book of Lemmas. Two lines from T just touch the circle; a third line through T crosses it. A chord drawn parallel to that third line looks ordinary, but the perpendicular dropped from a certain point always lands on its exact middle. Drag the dots and see if you can break it.

The lines in the picture

O is the centre and Bo fixes the radius. T is outside the circle, so exactly two tangents from it touch the circle at A and B. The line TC cuts the circle at C and again at C₂. BD is the chord through B parallel to TC, and AD meets TC at E. EH is drawn perpendicular to BD.

TA and TB touch the circle  ·  BD ∥ TC  ·  E = AD ∩ TC  ·  EH ⊥ BD

Angles that keep appearing

The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the opposite arc: ∠TAB = ∠ADB. Because BD is parallel to TC, that same angle is ∠AET. The two tangents from one point are equal, so ∠ABT = ∠TAB. Those equal angles put A, E, B and T on one circle — the shorter version of the proof that Nathan Bowler suggested on the original page.

E is as far from B as from D

Triangles EAT and AFT share the angle at T and have ∠TAB = ∠AET, so they are similar. That gives ET · TF = TA², and the tangent lengths give TA² = TB². This is the power of the point T. It makes triangles EBT and BFT similar, so ∠TEB = ∠TBF = ∠TAB. With the parallels this becomes ∠EDB = ∠EBD.

The altitude of an isosceles triangle

So triangle EBD has two equal base angles and therefore EB = ED. In an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from the top corner is also the median: BH = HD. The logic test checks that equality and every angle above over hundreds of configurations. It skips secants so close to a tangent that the chord is under two units long: the original applet's own "other intersection" routine works to one pixel and cannot tell the two ends apart there. The applet also chooses which tangent is called A and which B by an axis-based order; the claim holds with either naming.

Try dragging C almost onto A or B. The chord shrinks and the marks crowd together — then pull T far away and try again.
